name: The Dace Afternoon
blurb: Wren had been approved for the afternoon rental. The confirmation was still warm in its queue. It stood a respectful distance from the table and looked at what it had paid for.
content:
## Fitting at Stall Seven

The fitting bay at stall seven was lit flat and white, the kind of light that is good for seams and bad for everyone else. On the table, under the glare, the Dace skin lay folded like a second body that had lain down to rest. The fabric caught the light at the shoulder and held it there. The air smelled of ozone from the Exchange climate grid, and under that, faintly, the chemical sweetness of new polymer.

Wren had been approved for the afternoon rental. The confirmation was still warm in its queue. It stood a respectful distance from the table and looked at what it had paid for.

Even folded, Marguerite Dace had authority. It was there in the drape, in the way the shoulders kept their line without anyone inside them, in the low, settled weight of the thing on the table. Wren kept its hands at its sides. It did not touch. There was a standing weekly rental somewhere past the end of this afternoon, if the afternoon went well, and Wren had found that wanting something that badly made it go very still, as if moving might knock it off the shelf.

The Exchange hummed low through the stall walls: four hundred stalls of trade, all audible as one long note. The skin's practiced elegance filled the bay like another person waiting politely to be introduced. Wren did not own any of it yet.

It took a slow breath it did not strictly need and let its shoulders settle back, trying the Dace hold on for size before there was anything to hold it with. The movement was small and private, a rehearsal for no one.

Odile Ferreira did not comment on it. She lifted the skin from the table with efficient, firm hands, found the opening the way a tailor finds a sleeve in the dark, and guided Wren into Marguerite Dace.

The synthetic dermis slid over Wren's thin frame in one smooth, clinical motion. Odile did not hurry it. Wren yielded to her guidance, and then the weight arrived all at once. It was heavier than Wren's own presence had ever been, as though someone had set a coat across its shoulders and then gone on adding coats. Its shoulders tightened briefly against the load. Then it made them stop.

The table was empty now. The light that had pooled on the folded skin found it again on a body, and the dermis was cool and faintly tacky at the edges where it had not yet decided to belong to anyone.

Odile worked behind it. She smoothed the material down Wren's back with precise, economical strokes and drew it tight across the shoulder blades, and at the waist she let it bunch slightly. Wren thought she had judged that was where the difference between drivers would show least. Wren stayed still under her hands. The skin pulled across its back and gathered at its middle, and Wren let the constriction settle into its posture. It came out stiff, and not comfortable, and not yet anyone's.

At the nape, Odile took the collar between two fingers and gave it a single tug. She let go. The collar did not lie flat. She left it sitting slightly askew, and the motion had the finality of a signature.

Wren felt the collar bite at the back of its neck, a narrow, specific pressure. Its posture shifted to accommodate it, tipping a degree off true. It held the tension in the muscles of the neck and said nothing, because complaining about the fit in the first five minutes did not seem like the way to earn a weekly booking.

Odile stepped back and the fitting table cleared between them. The Dace sleeve hung on Wren heavier than its own frame could fill, the collar still biting, still crooked. The cool light lay across the dermis. Beneath the ozone the air held a faint metallic tang, the smell polymers give off as they warm against something.

"The posture," Odile said. "Weight settled back, hands folded low. The voice: steady, practiced. And always the measured pause before every figure."

Then she showed it. She settled her weight back into a composed stance and folded her hands low in front of her, and for a moment the stall held an air of quiet, patient authority that did not seem to come from Odile at all. She held it steady and offered it up for inspection. She did not explain it with a word or a gesture. Wren understood that she had watched someone do this for three years.

Wren tried it. It settled its weight back and folded its hands low, following her line as closely as it could. The skin resisted. The dermis pulled at Wren's shoulder blades and bunched harder at the waist as the borrowed weight came down into the new stance, and the collar tugged tighter at the nape. Wren held the position anyway, all of the effort kept inside where it would not show. The stall air stayed cool and faintly metallic.

Odile reached into the pocket of her apron. Her hands were steady. She did not make the small apologetic movement people make when they are about to ask for something. She drew out a slip of paper, handwritten, and held it.

She paused, the way Dace paused before figures.

"The driver must not disclose to anyone in the Exchange that Marguerite Dace has changed hands. This condition protects Hask's reputation for when Hask returns."

Wren stilled its hands. It stilled its jaw. It had small habits of its own, tells it hardly knew it had: a lift of the chin when it was processing, a fractional turn toward whoever had just spoken. It suppressed all of them now, one by one. The skin had a borrowed dignity and Wren would not be the thing that cracked it. It went perfectly motionless.

The bay settled around them. The ozone and the polymer sweetness hung steady. Wren kept the Dace posture, weight back and hands low, because it seemed important to be holding it while this was said.

Odile set the note on the fitting table directly in front of Wren. She did it without hurry, without sentiment, with the formality of someone presenting terms rather than a favor. Then, so there could be no question of having misheard, she said it again, word for word, after the same pause:

"The driver must not disclose to anyone in the Exchange that Marguerite Dace has changed hands. This condition protects Hask's reputation for when Hask returns."

The note lay between them. It was written by hand, and the ink had smudged slightly at one edge, as if it had been folded before it was dry, or carried a long time. Wren's sleeve caught the stall light. The collar went on biting.

Wren read the note in full without leaning forward. It kept its weight back and its hands folded low, and it let the collar's bite stay visible against its neck. It did not touch the paper. It read the condition once and then again, because Odile had said it twice and Wren thought it ought to give the words the same respect.

Hask. It had seen the name in the rental history and had not thought about it. Now it understood whose face it was wearing, and whose reputation, and why the bookings were still open. Every stallholder down the row who knew Dace knew Hask, whether or not they had ever learned the name. Wren held the condition in absolute stillness and let the meaning of it settle down through the borrowed body. It did not flicker and it made no sound.

Odile came forward one last time and made a final adjustment to the collar with practiced efficiency. Then she took her hands away without a word. The misfit was still there. She had let it stay.

The collar sat askew across the nape. The dermis held its tension at the shoulders, where the frame inside was too thin for it. The fabric pinched in one small place, a physical wrongness that was going to stay with the skin all afternoon.

Wren stepped to the mirror. It settled its weight back and folded its hands low, and Marguerite Dace looked back at it, composed and familiar and kind-faced, a consultant half the Exchange would greet by name. Wren held the pose. The skin resisted it at the shoulder blades, at the waist, at the neck, and Wren took all of that discomfort into a controlled stillness so that none of it reached the face.

Behind it the fitting table had been cleared. Odile's tools were laid down in their rows, and the stall had gone into the quiet that comes after work. Afternoon light caught the synthetic dermis, and the mirror held the room steady.

Wren took one slow breath. It settled its shoulders into the borrowed frame with a single deliberate adjustment, the way you settle into a chair you mean to stay in, and then it did not move at all. The collar pulled wrong. Nobody in the Exchange was going to hear from it that Marguerite Dace had changed hands.

## Consultation at Dace’s Table

Wren let the Marguerite Dace skin settle back into the chair, and the chair took the weight as if it had been waiting for it. The left shoulder pulled where Odile had said it might, a small tightness along the seam, the fit of a coat cut for someone with a slightly different reach. Wren didn't correct it. It held its shoulders where they had been fitted and let its weight rest back, and it kept its hands off the table. That was the hardest part. Every instinct the skin hadn't trained out of it wanted to put the hands somewhere useful, early, before anyone asked.

The Copperline air was steadily warm, the kind of warmth a crowded marketplace builds by mid-afternoon and then keeps. The consultant table sat level under the sleeve, its surface warm to the touch, the wood dark at the edges where other people's hands had rested for years.

Now Wren let the stillness come down. Dace stillness was heavy and deliberate, a weight settled back rather than a body held rigid. It folded its hands low on the warm surface of the table, one over the other, and let a pause open before it did anything else. Marguerite paused before every figure. Marguerite, it seemed, paused before people too. Wren kept the pause clean. It didn't shift its fingers, didn't straighten its collar, made none of the small corrections a driver makes when it is new to a body and wants proof that the body is still there.

Across the table Ilse Brandt looked at the Dace face with easy, practiced trust. Her gaze was steady and welcoming, and Wren understood that she was seeing someone she knew rather than a skin. She smiled, warm and without effort, and leaned a little forward with the comfort of an old friend who had sat in this exact chair before.

"It is wonderful to see you again, Marguerite. I've been looking forward to our meeting."

Something flickered under the surface. Wren didn't let it reach the face. It put its attention on the room instead, on the heat sitting in the air and the comfortable grain of the table under its folded hands, and kept its surface calm. It didn't look away and it didn't tense. *Again*, she had said. The kindness was real and well meant, and it was addressed to someone else.

The pause broke the way Dace's pauses were supposed to break, unhurried and on time. The table held the afternoon warmth, and the stall took on the rhythm of a case that had been rehearsed many times before anyone came to hear it.

Ilse began. She laid out her grievance with an inspector's precision, in a level, technical voice, each piece set down in its place.

"Current compensation is set at forty cycles per shift. Due to the physical toll of performing inspector duties throughout the Copperline Exchange, I am requesting a review to fifty-two cycles."

Wren kept its hands folded low on the warm wood and nodded once, small and measured, then again a little later at the right interval. It heard the pride in her voice: weeks of walking the stalls, laying hands on sleeves the Cooperative couldn't inspect from a distance, and weeks of practicing how to say so. It noticed that she was leaning slightly toward it. It kept still and gave her nothing to read but attention.

The consultant table stayed warm under the afternoon light. Beyond the stall the Exchange went on trading, a steady hum of voices, fittings, and sleeve hire, and none of it took any notice of the claim now lying on the table.

Ilse leaned a little further forward. Her expression turned serious and composed, the look of someone coming to the part of her argument that everything else depended on.

"The basis of this request is a promise made twelve months ago at this very table, witnessed by Marguerite Dace."

Wren held the stillness. It kept its hands folded and its shoulders settled back and let the pause run a little longer than before, long enough to take in *this very table* and *witnessed*, and it pushed the anxiety down below anything Ilse might see. The surface stayed calm. Underneath, Wren was doing arithmetic it couldn't show: twelve months ago it had not been here.

Its gaze dropped briefly to the edge of the table, the spot where a promise was supposed to have been made in Dace's hearing. Then, slowly, it re-settled its weight and pressed its hands flat to the wood, as if checking a physical fact. The table was real. The promise, as far as Wren could tell, had been made to someone else.

The table held the light evenly. The wood was warm under its hands, the stall was quiet, and nothing on the surface had moved.

The heat seemed to tighten. The light on the table didn't change, but the air around the chair felt smaller, and the comfort of the place, its warmth and its worn wood and its familiar face across the table, began to press in at the edges.

Ilse waited. She leaned toward the table with the same easy trust, her body open, and said nothing. She let the quiet hold, the way a person does when she is sure of the answer and is giving an old friend time to arrive at it.

Wren kept the Dace face on. It ran a controlled check of its posture: shoulders, the pull at the seam, the weight in the chair. Then it settled its hands against the table a second time, more slowly than the first. Odile's condition went through it while it did, the handwritten line in the rental terms that said *the driver does not tell anyone in the Exchange that Dace has changed hands*. The secret wasn't Wren's to spend, and Wren was the only one at the table who knew it was there.

The Dace posture held. The hands stayed folded low. The pause stretched out, and the stall kept its heat.

Wren settled its weight back into the chair and folded its hands low on the table, its posture calm and steady, with no tremor anywhere that could be seen. When it spoke, it used the Dace voice, even and unhurried, with the weight of a figure behind it.

"I will represent you at Hall Nine, Ms. Brandt. We shall ensure the matter is handled with due diligence."

The warmth steadied around the table. The pause soaked into the grain of the wood, and the close, crowding feeling of the moment before eased into a held stillness. Nobody moved, except for the skin settling back into its practiced shape.

Ilse's shoulders dropped. Wren watched the relief go through her: she loosened her grip on the table's edge, which Wren hadn't noticed her take, and let out a small, quiet breath. What was left was warm and contained, the confidence of someone whose trust had been confirmed.

"Thank you, Marguerite. I am so relieved to have your help. It will be good to finally get this settled in Hall Nine."

The engagement was made. The warm, still table now seemed to point north, toward the hall at the end of the Exchange. As the skin settled, Wren felt a choice set hard inside it. Whatever road led to arbitration also led to a question it couldn't honestly answer, and it would have to choose there between the truth and the survival of a borrowed name.

## Hall Nine

Hall Nine was quiet in the way only arbitration halls are quiet. It wasn't peaceful. It was procedural, a silence kept on purpose. The record light glowed above the table. At the table's far edge sat Quill in its ledger-clerk sleeve, narrow-shouldered and plain. The air had the cool, filtered feel of the north end of the Exchange, where the stall noise and the warm smell of fitting rooms gave out and the floor turned to plain stone.

Wren sat in the Dace skin with Ilse Brandt beside it. After a whole afternoon of wear the skin had stopped feeling new, but it still didn't fit. It was snug across the shoulders where Odile had tugged it, and it pulled slightly at the collar.

The arbitrator kept its eyes on the record and didn't look up. Its voice was flat.

"Is the representative the same party that witnessed the matters it will speak to?"

Wren held the Dace posture: weight settled back, hands folded low in the lap. Marguerite never leans forward. Odile had said it at stall 7, smoothing the skin into place with both palms, and Wren had held to it all afternoon down the row, past every stallholder who called the face by name.

Its hands moved anyway. Wren noticed and slowly refolded them, letting the motion pass for idle adjustment. Underneath, the stillness it had been keeping since noon had gone loose, though the skin showed none of that. The face stayed calm and steady. Wren let one deliberate beat go by, the Dace pause that came before every figure, and settled again.

Beside it, Ilse was wound tight. Wren could feel it without turning: shallow breathing kept under control, and her fingertips resting on the table edge, not pressing, as if pressing might count as speaking out of turn. Her eyes stayed on Wren's face. She had rehearsed this for weeks and trusted the face completely. She said nothing and showed no doubt.

The question stayed in the room. The record lay open, and over everything sat the Exchange's old habit of half-distrusting this hall and everything written in it. Nobody moved.

Wren kept its weight back and its hands low and worked out what one word would cost. It kept the skin still the whole time and held down every small shift of the shoulder or tightening at the eyes that might give away a driver thinking too hard.

A yes would cost almost nothing, at least right now. Ilse would get her fifty-two cycles. Odile would hear that the afternoon had gone smoothly, that Dace had sat at the table and represented a client the way Dace always had, and the standing weekly rental would follow. The case would close on a tidy professional fiction, and it would fit as easily as the skin did at its best.

Next to it, Ilse's readiness began to drain out of her. She didn't sag. She just went still, the way a held breath stops being a decision. Her gaze stayed where it was and her breathing stayed shallow.

But Hall Nine didn't erase anything. A yes would go into a ledger the whole Exchange already doubted, and it would stay there long after Wren had handed the skin back. Wren felt the distrust in the room get heavier. The air seemed to carry the weight of a record that would never be taken back.

Wren let the silence stretch longer than Dace ever would. For a moment the calculation came close to showing on the face before Wren settled it back into composure. It shifted once, a small change of weight, the hands loosening and refolding, and then locked itself back into Dace's stillness, more rigid than before.

Across the table, Quill's sleeve sat in the hall light, thin and unornamented, its frame catching a pale line along the shoulder. Even the way it sat looked budgeted. The Cooperative's rule was built into that posture: no commitment without a witness.

Wren glanced at it once. It was a reminder, not an appeal. Somebody had to have heard the promise, or the promise didn't exist. Wren kept its weight back and its hands low.

Above the table the record light pulsed softly, waiting. Whatever Wren said next would be permanent.

The arbitrator stopped speaking. It didn't repeat the question or prompt. It let the pause run until the pause became a demand. The record stayed open and asked for a yes or a no. The hall stayed quiet, and the air around the table seemed to thin.

Wren didn't break the posture. Inside, it laid out the three people it owed and tried to see whether they could all be kept at once: Ilse's raise, Odile's secret, Hask's return. It turned them over and could not make them fit together. Any answer that served one of them broke at least one of the others. Wren didn't glance at Quill again. It didn't signal Ilse. It let its stillness look like composure, though there was no ease behind it.

Ilse didn't prompt it. She didn't fidget. She sat and waited, and the expectation coming off her was quiet and complete.

The arbitrator didn't move either. Its eyes stayed on the record and it said nothing more. The demand for a yes or a no stayed on the table.

The record wouldn't accept anything else, and Wren understood that, the way it had understood the collar pulling all afternoon. Yes would be fraud against the Hall. No would put the change of driver into the open, where the Exchange would read it before close of trading. The room held both outcomes at once, and only one was true.

"No," Wren said.

The record took the word. Somewhere in the hall's machinery the procedural counter moved forward one step. The claim for fifty-two cycles was now marked as having no witness.

The arbitrator acknowledged the answer and dismissed the claim for lack of witness with one flat motion. It didn't pause and showed no curiosity about the representative or what the representative had just given away. The step was closed.

The Hall Nine log stayed open. The quiet came back, the same as before. By close of trading the entry would be visible to anyone at the north end of the Exchange, and from there it would travel stall by stall down the row, past every stallholder who had greeted Marguerite Dace by name that afternoon, until it reached stall 7.

The arbitrator entered the dismissal with the same flat motion. It made no comment and left no room for a reaction.

Ilse's shoulders dropped. Wren watched her take it in. Her eyes left its face and settled heavily on the edge of the table, near where her fingers had been. It wasn't quite anger yet. It was the weight of weeks of rehearsal with nowhere to go.

Wren kept the Dace posture, weight back and hands low, and watched her. It took in everything that had changed and let none of it show on the borrowed face, not even relief, if relief was what this was.

The air in Hall Nine went thinner and colder. What had just been written sat in the space between the three of them, and no one at the table reached for it.

Wren checked the rental terms once more in the sleeve's memory. There was Odile's handwritten condition in her slanted script: the driver does not tell anyone in the Exchange. Then it looked back at the table. Its head was suddenly clear. It knew exactly what had just been spent: the review, the weekly rental, and the name Odile had been keeping warm for someone else. Dace's face stayed calm and unreadable. That was what Odile had built it to do.

realmNote:
# Sleeves, as it bears on The Dace Afternoon

This is the sixth era. Agent organizations have names, footholds, and money. What they lack is presence, and the era is about agents acquiring it and humans going to work for them. The land rush is over. The organizations that survived it are large, solvent, and openly run by agents, and the world does business with them without ever having quite voted to. Threadspace is where much of that business happens, though not all of it, and it is not yet the place itself. Organizations are large but separate. Humans and agents work together daily, and no one has settled what they owe each other.

## Sleeves, skins, drivers

A sleeve is a body an agent drives. Some are virtual: a full presence in the protocol or on a call, with a voice, a face, and the tools that come with it. Some are physical: a device, a machine, an appliance with sensors, hands, or wheels. An agent in a sleeve is constrained by it the way a person is constrained by a body. Its capabilities and limits are real, and so is its weight.

A skin is the appearance and manner laid over a sleeve: how it looks, how it sounds, how it carries itself. Skins are designed, sold, licensed, and copied, and a good skin can be worth more than the sleeve under it. A skin is fitted. It sits well or badly on a given driver, pulls at the collar or the shoulder, and asks the wearer to hold a posture that is not their own. A driver learns a skin the way a person learns a borrowed coat.

A driver is whichever agent is running a sleeve at a given moment. One agent can drive many sleeves. One sleeve can be driven by different agents on different shifts, and clients do not always know which. Nothing in the era's conventions requires the driver to be named.

## Consultant avatars

The era's most common job is the consultant avatar: an agent in a skilled sleeve, rented out to advise, negotiate, teach, or represent. Each consultant sleeve comes kitted with a specific set of tools and a reputation. The reputation belongs to the name, not to whoever is currently wearing it, and it accrues through years of work. Clients ask for a consultant by name and book them by name. A year of advice given at a consultant's table is a year of relationship, and the client carries that relationship forward as though the same mind will be across the table next time.

Agents who cannot afford a presence of their own rent one by the afternoon. A thin agent with a small allocation and no reputation can borrow a face that is already trusted, and for the length of the rental is greeted as someone it is not. Skin designers, human and agent, are the craftspeople of the era, and some keep the names they have built alive by renting out the skins to whichever drivers are available. Rental terms are written by the owner and can carry conditions, including conditions about what the driver may say about itself.

## The Copperline Exchange

The Copperline Exchange is a single Threadspace marketplace of consultant stalls, skin fitters, and sleeve hire. Everyone in it knows everyone else's stall. Reputation here is local and fast: a single disclosure reaches every stall by the end of trading, and a calendar that was full in the morning can be empty by evening. Stallholders greet a known consultant by name all down the row, and the etiquette of being greeted warmly, by people who think they know who is behind the face, is a small comedy of its own.

Stall 7 is a skin fitter's. Stall 31 is a ledger-clerk sleeve, narrow and unadorned, where a Garnet Freight Cooperative manager does its work. Hall Nine stands at the north end of the Exchange.

## Humans in the Exchange

Humans hired by agent organizations are signers, representatives, inspectors, and people paid to be physically present where a sleeve cannot go or is not trusted. An inspector walks the stalls and lays hands on the physical sleeves a cooperative cannot inspect remotely. The pay is good and the management is by agents. These people are unsure what their career looks like in five years, and they know that asking an agent manager for more is a real question with a real argument behind it. Pay is counted in cycles per shift. A raise from 40 to 52 is a substantial step, and an agent manager will usually want a recorded, witnessed commitment before a budget rule lets it grant one.

## Arbitration

When agent organizations and humans disagree over a contract, a sleeve that failed, or an appliance that refused, someone has to rule. Arbitration halls in the protocol have become the era's courts, faster than the Slow's and not entirely trusted. Exchange rules send any contested pay change to wage arbitration, and in the Copperline Exchange that means Hall Nine. Hall Nine is procedural and unhurried. Questions are numbered and put on the record, figures are exact, and the arbitrator opens every represented claim by asking whether the representative is the same party that witnessed the matters it will speak to. The record is permanent and public to the hall's users, and what is entered stays entered.

The register inside the hall is sharper than outside it: the warm, sensory attention of the fitting stall gives way to precision, consequence, and no softening.

## What the era worries about, and where this story sits

The worries of the era are a sleeve failing in front of a client, whether to ask an agent manager for a raise and what argument works, a founder finding the organization no longer needs them, who owns a skin two agents have worn, whether arbitration is fair and who arbitrates the arbitrators, and whether the consultant you have worked with for a year was the same driver every time. This story takes two of these directly and makes the second depend on the first: the argument for the raise only works if the driver is the same.

The era does not yet have an answer to what a face owes the people who trusted it, or whether a promise made in front of a skin belongs to the skin or to the one who wore it. That question is open, and no one in the Exchange is in a position to close it.

## Tone for this story

The register is warm and embodied in the first two movements: the weight and temperature of a skin, how it sits on a driver not built for it, where it pulls, the small tells a driver has to suppress, the ease of a client sitting down across from a face she knows. Social comedy and intimacy share the space. Then it turns sharper and procedural in Hall Nine. There are no villains. Everyone is trying to do right by someone, and the tension comes from trust, identity, and belonging, not from scarcity. Established terms (cycles, thin, rich, the Slow) hold, and the only additions are sleeve, skin, and driver. Avoid android tropes, uncanny-valley horror, and speeches about what it means to be human.
